# How to Make AI Videos with Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash in Picsart

> **In short:** Google says Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash is now available in Picsart AI Playground. You can test ideas in quick, low-resolution 360p drafts, then render the take you like at 1080p or 4K. This guide walks you through the process in five steps.

Have you ever had a short video idea you wanted to test before spending real time on it? Maybe it's a product clip for a small shop, a teaser for a family project, or a few seconds of a story you keep imagining. This guide shows you how to try those ideas quickly with an AI video model, which is a program that creates moving pictures from a written description.

## What you need before you start

Check these three things before Step 1:

- **A Picsart account and access to AI Playground.** AI Playground is the part of Picsart where you can use AI models. If you're new to the app, Picsart's help pages explain how to get set up.
- **Credits.** Each generation uses Picsart credits, which are a usage balance the platform tracks. The cost is shown before anything runs, so you can decide whether to continue.
- **A short scene idea.** A few sentences describing a beginning, a middle, and an end are enough to start.

Google's announcement describes Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash as a model built for fast drafts and for finished, high-quality output. This guide covers the workflow it describes. Menu labels and limits can change, so when your screen looks different, trust what Picsart shows you and check its current help pages.

## Step 1 — Open the model in AI Playground

Open Picsart and go to AI Playground. Look for the place where you choose a model, and select Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash. Once it's chosen, the settings for your video should appear. If you can't find the model, check Picsart's help pages before you assume it's unavailable, because labels on the screen may differ from the wording in this guide.

💬 Example: Select "Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash" as the model before you write anything.

**You'll know it worked when** the model name is selected and the video settings (format, length, and prompt box) are showing on your screen.

## Step 2 — Set the shape and length

Pick the format that fits where your video will be posted. Google's announcement suggests 9:16 (tall, vertical) for Reels, TikTok, and YouTube Shorts, and 16:9 (wide, horizontal) for YouTube and TV. Then choose a length. According to the announcement, you can set anything from 3 to 15 seconds, and 15 seconds is the longest a single generation can run now, up from 10. That gives you room for one complete moment of action instead of a fragment.

💬 Example: Choose 9:16 and set the length to 8 seconds for a quick phone clip.

**You'll know it worked when** your chosen shape and length are set before you write your prompt, so you're not guessing later.

## Step 3 — Write your prompt and add references

A **prompt** is the instruction you type to the AI, describing what you want to see. Write about a beginning, a middle, and an end, rather than one frozen picture. Then name one camera move, such as a slow push-in or a slow turn around an object. If something must look the same from shot to shot, like a person, a product, or a logo, attach it as a **reference**. A reference is a file, such as a photo or short clip, that shows the AI what to keep consistent. The announcement says you can attach up to five image references and three video references.

💬 Example prompt: "Vertical 9:16, 8 seconds. A ceramic coffee mug sits on a wooden table by a window. Morning light moves across it and steam rises. The camera slowly pushes in on the handle. Keep the mug's glaze and color exactly as in the reference photo."

**You'll know it worked when** your prompt describes a sequence, and any reference files you need are attached before you run the draft.

## Step 4 — Draft at 360p

Run your first generations at 360p. Google's announcement calls this draft mode, a fast, lower-cost pass for testing ideas before the final render. Create several versions with small changes, such as a different opening shot or a different pace. Keep going until one version feels right. Drafting first is the easiest way to find your best idea before you spend credits on a sharper render.

💬 Example: Keep the same prompt, but change only the first sentence ("Start on a close-up of the handle"), then run it again so you can compare the two drafts.

**You'll know it worked when** you have two or three rough clips to compare, and one of them clearly stands out as the strongest idea.

## Step 5 — Render your favorite take in 1080p or 4K

When you've picked a take, render that one at higher quality. The announcement says final renders can go up to 4K, which is sharp enough for large screens and long series. It also describes 720p as a good middle step for sharing a cut with a friend or teammate for feedback, and 1080p as a fit for finished social posts. Higher resolution generally costs more credits, so check the displayed cost before you confirm.

💬 Example: Render the chosen take in 1080p for a social post, or in 4K if it's headed for a TV or a large screen.

**You'll know it worked when** the final clip is ready at the resolution you picked and looks sharp when you play it back.

## Common mistakes

- **Rendering in high resolution too early.** It's tempting to jump straight to 4K, but that spends credits on ideas you haven't tested. **Fix:** draft every idea at 360p first, and render only the take you keep.
- **Writing one frozen moment.** A prompt like "a woman smiling" gives the AI very little to work with. **Fix:** describe a beginning, a middle, and an end, and add one camera move.
- **Skipping references when things must match.** If your character or product changes between shots, the clip can look inconsistent. **Fix:** attach image or video references for anything that has to stay the same.
- **Choosing the wrong shape.** A wide clip posted to a vertical feed gets cropped or looks awkward. **Fix:** pick 9:16 for phone-first platforms and 16:9 for YouTube and TV before you generate.

## What this means for you

- **In everyday life**: If you make family videos, school projects, or hobby clips, you can test a few versions of a short scene in minutes and keep only the one you like best.
- **If you run a small shop or side project**: You can draft several short clips from one simple brief, compare the openings, and render only the strongest. Keep your product photos handy, because they work well as references.
- **If you're just getting started**: Begin with one 5-second clip in 9:16 at 360p. Write three sentences: a beginning, a middle, and an end. That's enough to learn how the drafts behave.
- **If you already use it**: Attach a product photo as a reference, ask for a slow turn around the product, and compare your 360p drafts to see how well the product's details hold up before you render in 4K.

## Wrap-up

Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash, as Google describes it, lets you draft in Picsart AI Playground at 360p, add references to keep people and products consistent, and render your best take in up to 4K. Your next step is simple: open AI Playground today, choose the model, and make one 5-second draft. Once you've seen a few drafts side by side, you'll know which idea deserves the full render.
